name: Vesilute

lead: Vesilute is a very short peptide, glutamic acid joined to aspartic acid, from the Khavinson bioregulator tradition developed in St. Petersburg.
People interested in longevity use it as part of a wellness routine aimed at the bladder and urinary tract, with some mentions of prostate comfort.

paras: Proponents say the dipeptide supports bladder tissue, smooth muscle and regeneration. The mechanism has not been described in published human studies.
Clinical evidence is limited and it is sold mainly through research-peptide vendors. Regulatory status varies and was not specified by the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Proponents position Vesilute as one piece of a longevity stack aimed at urinary and pelvic health. Any effect on looks is a downstream claim about overall vitality rather than a direct change to appearance.

lead: Vesilute is a synthetic dipeptide made of glutamic acid and aspartic acid (Glu-Asp, often abbreviated "ED"), described as a Khavinson-style peptide bioregulator developed at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology [1]. Sellers and peptide-database pages describe it as aimed at bladder and urinary tract tissue [1].

People in longevity and peptide circles use it as part of a general-wellness routine aimed at urinary and pelvic health, which proponents link to comfort, vitality and staying active. Some pages also mention prostate support for men [1]. Its connection to appearance is indirect and claimed rather than direct.
The published research base is small. The database page that lists it cites three general reviews and itself states that clinical evidence is limited [1].
infobox: St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology [1]

paras: Vesilute is a two-amino-acid peptide built from glutamic acid and aspartic acid [1]. It belongs to the family of short peptide bioregulators associated with Vladimir Khavinson's group, each of which is marketed as supporting a particular organ or tissue [1].

Vendor and database pages describe it as supporting bladder and urinary tract function, smooth muscle regulation, pelvic blood flow and tissue regeneration; some list prostate comfort for men as an emerging area [1].
No studies found. The database page that lists Vesilute cites general reviews of the Khavinson peptide family rather than trials of this dipeptide, and describes clinical evidence as limited [1].
Vesilute is sold mainly by research-peptide vendors and discussed on peptide blogs and database sites. Regulatory status is not addressed on the pages reviewed [1].
